strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaborative workflows affect human-in-the-loop qualitative coding. Its focus on researcher interaction and downstream codebooks is clearly motivated.

The comparison spans three substantially different system families, 15 coding sessions, and a common corpus of approximately 85,000 tweets. Shared initializations within systems provide useful control for an exploratory comparison.

The evaluation distinguishes consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and assignment correctness. Manually checking 1,200 document-theme pairs with two annotators and adjudication provides valuable evidence beyond embedding metrics; reporting Krippendorff’s alpha is also helpful.

The exposition is generally clear. Appendices provide prompts, several configuration details, hardware, and runtime information, while participant observations identify concrete usability problems involving agency and refinement operations.
weaknesses: The central experimental comparison does not isolate collaboration modality. Section 2 defines asynchronous collaboration as independent coding followed by consolidation, but Section 4 compares unconsolidated individual codebooks with codebooks produced by three-person synchronous teams. Team size and potentially human effort therefore change alongside synchrony. Participant expertise, allocation, and session duration are insufficiently controlled or reported. The study needs a matched collaborative comparison or an explicit reframing as exploratory individual-versus-group coding.

The statistical evidence does not establish the claimed significant effects. Each system has only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks, yielding one synchronous codebook pair and three overlapping asynchronous pairs. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying sample sizes or the analysis unit. Treating themes or matches as independent would ignore their dependence within codebooks and shared comparisons. Experimental-unit-aware uncertainty, participant reuse information, and treatment of multiple comparisons are needed; 'near statistically significant' results provide weak support.

Correctness reporting contains a consequential ambiguity and inconsistency. Figure 4 reports F1, but the paper does not define how document-theme validity judgments produce that score, including its averaging convention. The claim that asynchronous topic modeling produces more accurate assignments is not supported consistently by the figure: both settings reach approximately 0.50 overall, and synchronous coding is higher at the middle cumulative thresholds. Confidence intervals and a clear account of quartile aggregation are needed before interpreting modality differences.

The proposed evaluation framework needs stronger justification as a measure of codebook quality. Best-match averaging leaves handling of unequal theme counts and unmatched themes unclear, and actual theme counts and size distributions are absent. Selecting the closest quartile using embeddings also makes increased embedding cohesion partly expected by construction. Uniform sampling across themes requires appropriate weighting to support corpus-level correctness claims. Moreover, Table 4 reports 0.7–16.1% invalid-label outputs, without explaining their treatment in the main comparisons.

Several conclusions exceed the tested conditions. Broad claims about LLM unreliability and scalability rest on one Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct configuration with explanation-generating prompts; one candidate prompt even contains programming-oriented language about objects, classes, and code functionality. These results characterize this implementation, but do not establish general limitations of LLM-assisted coding. Likewise, interaction bandwidth is not independently manipulated, so its proposed explanatory role remains a hypothesis.

Reproducibility and qualitative-analysis reporting remain incomplete. The design entails 27 participant-session slots but reports 20 participants without explaining reuse or ordering. The exact S-BERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, selected prompt per session, prompt-selection sample sizes, and resulting codebooks are not supplied; analysis code and outputs are only promised. Appendix C acknowledges omitted interviews, but interview counts and analysis procedures are missing, and group versus individual interview formats complicate comparisons. Together with the design and inference concerns, these gaps require substantive revision before Findings-level soundness and reproducibility are established.
